decisions.reason: The cited definition is restricted to finite Q, so F2 overstated its scope; the correspondence itself is valid for arbitrary Q by the displayed identities. F2 now explicitly adopts the same equations as a local convention for arbitrary groups on the given nonzero finite-dimensional V. Multiplicativity of D, reconstruction of P, inverse constructions and intertwiners use no finiteness. This is a nonfatal definition-scope defect, not a reason to weaken the theorem.

The average in 1.4 originally used operators on V as if defined on M; thus the complement argument had an undefined load-bearing term. Defined P(q)m=u_q m on M first, checked C-linearity, the projective product and both inverse identities from the module law and cocycle, and only then averaged. Conjugation cancels the scalar cocycle and permutes Q, giving an A-linear projection. Finite dimension gives finite length, so the regular module is semisimple; zero M causes no difficulty. This repairs a fatal logic gap in the written proof.

The final clause of 5.2 confused the degree [H:H_theta] dim(sigma) with the multiplicity dim(sigma) of theta in restriction. For S3=C3 semidirect C2 at a nontrivial theta these are 2 and 1. Corrected only that clause; the degree formula was already proved correctly and the extension theta(ah)=theta(a), Gallagher bijection and Clifford induction establish the unchanged theorem. The erroneous side identification is nonfatal to its claimed parametrization.

The example had no specified normal-subgroup type to which its Clifford obstruction language applied. The scalar computation alpha_c(t,t)=i^2=-1 and alpha_c=delta c was sound. Specified G=C2, N={1}, and its unique irreducible rho on C: the given P and P_c restrict to rho and satisfy both N-compatibility identities, so they are inertia operators of the same type and its obstruction is zero. This repairs the nonfatal unsupported interpretation without changing the example.

The asserted criterion for a map C2 to C* was false: preserving identity alone does not imply multiplicativity. This was the written justification that the witness theta is a character, a fatal logic defect. Replaced it with all products: identity factors preserve values and theta((-1)^2)=1=theta(-1)^2. The resulting one-dimensional nonzero representation is irreducible, is invariant by centrality, and cannot extend since the explicit commutator [i,j]=-1 maps to 1 under every linear character.

F4 omitted V nonzero from the exact definition of irreducibility. Added that requirement; the intended converse already assumes an irreducible V and its orbit span contains the nonzero line Cv1. The coset functions have matrix entry lambda(h) when xt=tprime h, and the inverse maps Phi and Psi intertwine by that same formula. Also made the elementary coset partition argument explicit in F3 instead of attributing it to the bare coset definition. The missing qualification was nonfatal for these nonzero uses.

F6 cited a definition that only specifies the kernel set, not normality. This is nonfatal: the displayed calculation already proves centrality, which gives e k e^{-1}=k and hence normality. Removed the unsupported clause and supplied that direct argument; associativity, both inverse products, centrality and the quotient map hold for arbitrary Q.

F3 omitted V nonzero from the irreducibility definition. Added the missing condition; its sole application here is to C, which is one-dimensional and nonzero. Evaluation at 1 and v maps to (g maps to g^{-1}v) are inverse G-maps proving induction from G to itself is identity. The sum-of-squares formula and the one-dimensionality theorem then give the trivial and finite abelian cases. The restatement error is nonfatal to all three assertions.

The final summary incorrectly made the index-one inducing subgroup abelian. It must be U itself, which is nonabelian; only the degree-p characters use abelian H. Corrected that summary while retaining the exact p^2 and p-1 counts. Checked conjugation sends mu_{c,d} to mu_{c-dx,d}, so H is normal and each d nonzero gives one orbit with inertia H. Clifford induction and the squared-degree sum p^2+(p-1)p^2=p^3 prove completeness, including p=2. The erroneous summary adjective is nonfatal to the established classification.

every row and column, so monomial representations are precisely the
representation-theoretic form of the permutation-with-scalars pattern, and a

page_repairs.after:
every row and column. Conversely, an irreducible representation with this
permutation-with-scalars pattern is monomial: irreducibility forces the action
on its basis lines to be transitive. A linear character of $G$ is monomial
because induction from $G$ to itself is the identity.
page_repairs.reason: A monomial-matrix representation may have several orbits of basis lines; for example C^2 with trivial group action has such matrices but cannot be induced from a one-dimensional subgroup representation of the trivial group. Claim 2 supplies the converse only for an irreducible representation, whose orbit span is all of V. The summary now states that exact hypothesis.
